title: Basalt Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Basalt wells have a 102 ft median depth, with typical completed-well costs of $12,600-$22,200.
h1: Basalt, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
For rural property around Basalt, the well records point to generally productive mountain wells, but the ground is still highly local. The median reported depth is 102 feet, and the median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute. Most permits identify fractured bedrock rather than a uniform shallow aquifer.

This page covers permitted wells within five miles of Basalt in Eagle County. Use the numbers to frame a driller's bid and ask better questions, not to guarantee what a new well will do on one particular lot. Nearby records from El Jebel, Snowmass, Catherine, and other surrounding areas can help fill in the picture.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Basalt?
sections.html:
Reported well depths around Basalt have a 102-foot median. The middle half runs from 58 to 232 feet, meaning half of the wells with reported depths fall inside that range. The 90th-percentile depth is 350 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,030 feet.

The depth mix is useful when reviewing a bid: 48% are under 100 feet, 36% are 100 to 300 feet, 13% are 300 to 600 feet, and 3% exceed 600 feet. A site near the median may support a shorter initial drilling estimate, but fractured granite and gneiss can change the result quickly. Ask for pricing beyond the expected depth, plus casing, grout, pump, and testing assumptions.

sections.heading: What Basalt wells produce
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 12.2 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 27% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 3% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a favorable record for household planning, but a pump-yield figure is not the same as unlimited storage or guaranteed flow during every season. Only 447 wells report a yield, compared with 1,599 permits in the full record. Confirm the test method, recovery, storage tank size, and intended household demand before relying on a neighboring result.

sections.heading: Water levels in Basalt: useful, but not a straight trend
sections.html:
The median static water level is 63 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 28 to 182 feet. That range matters for pump selection and drilling cost because a deeper water level can require more lift even when the borehole itself is not unusually deep.

The decade figures do not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 36 feet in the 1990s, 152 feet in the 2010s, and 69 feet in the 2020s. Only 120 records report a static water level, and measurements may come from different locations and conditions. Treat the series as a reason to check current nearby measurements, not proof that the water table is steadily dropping or recovering.

sections.heading: Basalt permit history and the drillers in the records
sections.html:
The permit history is largest in the 1990s, with 434 permits. The record shows 236 from the 2000s, 149 from the 2010s, and 105 from the 2020s. Earlier decades include 189 permits in the 1980s, 173 in the 1970s, and 63 in the 1960s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Most permits are for domestic or household use at 71%. Irrigation accounts for 7%, stock for 5%, and monitoring for 15%. The most active names in these records are Shelton Drilling Corporation, with 523 wells; Collins Drilling Co, with 191; and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., with 166. These are record associations, not recommendations. Verify current licensing, availability, and scope before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Basalt well may cost
sections.html:
Basalt drilling commonly encounters fractured mountain bedrock described here as granite or gneiss. The cost model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 102-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $6,600 to $10,200.

A finished well is a larger project. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled total at the median depth is about $12,600 to $22,200. Depth is the major swing factor, but access, casing and grout requirements, water-level lift, and site trenching can also move the bid. Request a written allowance for each item and a clear per-foot price if the hole continues past the planned depth.

sections.heading: Basalt risks to check before you buy or build
sections.html:
Fractured-bedrock wells can vary sharply over short distances. A strong neighboring well does not guarantee the same result, and a poor result can mean low yield, a dry hole, or a deeper-than-planned bore. Review nearby permits and construction reports, especially around El Jebel, Snowmass, Catherine, Mulford, Carbondale, and Woody Creek, while giving the closest wells the most weight.

There are 7 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features within about 10 miles. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped search, but that does not replace a site-specific water test. Before construction, confirm well location, septic setbacks, access for a rig, electrical trench routes, and whether the intended household use is allowed by the permit. Colorado DWR records and an approved septic layout should be part of the due diligence file.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Basalt, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Basalt is 102 feet. The middle half ranges from 58 to 232 feet, while the 90th percentile is 350 feet. Forty-eight percent are under 100 feet, but fractured mountain bedrock means a specific lot can require substantially more drilling.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Basalt?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate in Basalt is $65-$100 per foot. At the 102-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $6,600-$10,200. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $12,600-$22,200. A deeper hole or difficult access can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Basalt wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 15.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 12.2 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent of reported wells exceed 15 gallons per minute. Only 447 wells report a yield, so ask for the actual test and recovery information rather than relying only on area statistics.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Basalt?
faq.a: The area records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. There are 7 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features within about 10 miles. Test the individual well for relevant contaminants, and retest after construction or changes in water quality. A permit record is not a drinking-water test.

faq.q: Are Basalt well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 36 feet in the 1990s, 152 feet in the 2010s, and 69 feet in the 2020s. Because only 120 records report static water levels and locations and conditions differ, use current nearby measurements to evaluate a property.
